title: The Honor of the Human Mind: Potsdam, the Albertina, and the Berlin Winter
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Potsdam: the Banker's Son and the Enforced Wait

stops.name: Potsdam, birth in the banker's house
stops.date_confidence: attested; MacTutor and both Wikipedia editions give 10 December 1804 at Potsdam. The coordinate is Potsdam's old town centre, not a verified birth address: no source consulted identifies the house or the street.
stops.campa: A second son is born to Simon Jacobi, a banker and money-changer of Potsdam, and to his wife Rachel Lehmann, in a prosperous Jewish household where books are ordinary furniture and the Prussian court sits half an hour up the road. The town is Frederick's town, laid out for garrisons and gardens. The family is not of it and not outside it. Some accounts give the child's first name as Jacques Simon; the name he will publish under, Carl Gustav Jacob, comes later, and the record does not agree about how much later.
suggested_refs: The Potsdam parish and civil registers of 1804, for the birth entry no reachable source quotes directly
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi'

stops.name: Potsdam, the uncle's lessons
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. MacTutor establishes home instruction by a maternal uncle before the boy entered school but gives no dates; the year here is set only to order the segment before the 1816 Gymnasium entry, and the uncle's given name is not established in any source consulted.
stops.campa: Before any school takes him, the boy is taught at home by an uncle on his mother's side, a Lehmann: classical languages on one side of the table and elementary mathematics on the other. He learns Greek and Latin as thoroughly as arithmetic, which is why, fourteen years on, the Prussian state will certify him to teach all of it. Nothing in the household marks him yet as a mathematician rather than a philologist. The uncle's given name is not recorded, and neither are the years the lessons ran.
suggested_refs: The Neue Deutsche Biographie notice on the Jacobi household, deutsche-biographie.de/gnd118775766.html
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi'

stops.name: Potsdam Gymnasium, promoted in six months and held four years
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by MacTutor, which places the entry shortly before his twelfth birthday of 10 December 1816; the month is inferred from that and is stated by no source. Coordinate approximate: the school he attended, the Grosse Stadtschule, later the Viktoria-Gymnasium and now the Helmholtz-Gymnasium, stood on what is today Friedrich-Ebert-Strasse and only moved to Kurfuerstenstrasse 53 in 1878, so the modern address is not the site he knew.
stops.campa: He enters the Gymnasium weeks before he turns twelve and is moved into the senior class within about six months. The school has nothing further to give him and cannot release him: the University of Berlin will not matriculate anyone under sixteen. So the boy who has finished the curriculum sits in the top form for four years, waiting on a birthday. The school's own published history still lists him among its pupils as one who reached university readiness at thirteen.
suggested_refs: Wikipedia (de), 'Helmholtz-Gymnasium Potsdam', for the school's sites and its list of pupils
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi'

stops.name: Potsdam Gymnasium, Euler and the quintic
stops.date_confidence: attested by MacTutor as belonging to the years of the enforced wait, 1816 to 1821; no source dates either the reading or the attempt more closely, and the year here only orders the segment.
stops.campa: In the four idle years he reads Euler's Introductio in analysin infinitorum, the book that had taught most of Europe what a function was, and then tries what nobody has managed: to solve the general equation of the fifth degree by radicals. He fails. He is a schoolboy in Potsdam and the thing is impossible, as Abel and Galois will shortly prove. The failure is not wasted; it shows him where the difficulty actually sits, which is not in his algebra. He goes up to Berlin in 1821 with the Introductio behind him and no result of his own.
suggested_refs: Leonhard Euler, Introductio in analysin infinitorum (Lausanne, 1748)
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi'

segments.name: The University of Berlin: Philology Set Aside

stops.name: Berlin, matriculation at the new university
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by MacTutor and both Wikipedia editions; month and day are not recorded and are defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: At sixteen he matriculates at the University of Berlin, itself only eleven years old, and divides himself between philosophy, classical philology, and mathematics. There is little advanced mathematics to hear in Prussia; the lectures assume less than he already knows. So he does in Berlin what he did in the Potsdam waiting room and reads: Euler, Lagrange, Laplace, Gauss. By 1823 he has stopped dividing himself and works at mathematics alone, taught by nobody in the building.
suggested_refs: The matriculation registers of the Friedrich-Wilhelms-Universitaet, Berlin, for 1821
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi'

stops.name: Berlin, the change of confession
stops.date_confidence: DISPUTED and deliberately left unresolved. MacTutor and English Wikipedia place the conversion around 1825, at the doctorate. German Wikipedia states flatly that he took the name Carl Gustav Jacob after converting to the evangelical Christian faith in his first semester, 1821. Deutsche Biographie gives only 'israelitisch, dann evangelisch' with no year at all. The date field carries the 1825 reading because the segment has to order on something; it is not settled, and the segment position should not be read as a finding.
stops.campa: He is baptized into the evangelical church and takes the name Carl Gustav Jacob. Whether this happens in his first semester at seventeen, or four years later at the threshold of a university career no Jew could then enter in Prussia, the sources do not agree, and the difference changes the meaning of the act entirely. A boy's conviction and a young man's calculation are not the same thing. The Berlin evangelical registers for 1821 and for 1825 would settle it. Neither has been quoted by anyone who writes about him.
suggested_refs: The baptismal registers of the Berlin evangelical parishes for 1821 and 1825, which would settle the question and which no reachable source quotes
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi'

stops.name: Berlin, the doctorate on partial fractions
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by MacTutor and both Wikipedia editions; month and day are not recorded and are defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: He submits Disquisitiones analyticae de fractionibus simplicibus, on the decomposition of rational fractions, and takes his doctorate at twenty. Habilitation follows almost immediately. The Prussian ladder that normally consumes a decade he climbs inside a single year, and he does it in a subject his own university barely teaches. He has been working alone since the Potsdam senior class, nine years, and the thesis is the first of that work anyone outside his own room has seen. He turns twenty-one in December.
suggested_refs: C. G. J. Jacobi, Disquisitiones analyticae de fractionibus simplicibus (Berlin, 1825)
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi'

stops.name: Berlin, the Academy declines the paper on iterated functions
stops.date_confidence: attested: MacTutor records that an 1825 paper on iterated functions was rejected by the Berlin Academy and was finally published, with commentary by Kurt-R. Biermann, in 1961. Month and day are not recorded and are defaulted to 01. Coordinate inherited byte-identically from leonard_euler.journey.json, the corpus pin for the Prussian Academy of Sciences.
stops.campa: In the same year the Berlin Academy is offered a paper of his on iterated functions and declines it. The manuscript goes into a drawer and stays there through his rise, his fame, his death, and four generations of German mathematics. No record survives of who read it for the Academy or of what was said against it. Kurt-R. Biermann prints it, with commentary, in 1961: a hundred and thirty-six years after it was written, a hundred and ten after the author died.
suggested_refs: Kurt-R. Biermann's 1961 edition of Jacobi's rejected 1825 paper on iterated functions
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi'

stops.name: Berlin, the Joachimsthalsches Gymnasium post
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by English Wikipedia, which also dates the Oberlehrer examination to autumn 1824; the month and day of the offer are not recorded and are defaulted to 01. The coordinate is the school's Burgstrasse 21-23 site in Berlin Mitte, where German Wikipedia places it from 1717 to 1880; the school moved to the Kaiserallee in Wilmersdorf in 1880 and only then to Templin in 1912, so neither later address is the building he was offered.
stops.campa: Having passed the Prussian state examination in autumn 1824, certified to teach mathematics, Greek, Latin, and history, he is offered a post at the Joachimsthalsches Gymnasium on the Burgstrasse. It is the respectable end of the road his uncle's lessons prepared him for: a schoolmaster of three subjects, secure for life, in the capital. He does not take it up. The doctorate is already in hand and the university is already the other option, and the classical training becomes a private accomplishment he never puts down. The school stays where it is on the Burgstrasse, as it has since 1717 and will until 1880.
suggested_refs: Wikipedia (de), 'Joachimsthalsches Gymnasium', for the school's Burgstrasse years
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi'

stops.name: Berlin, lecturing at twenty on curves and surfaces
stops.date_confidence: attested by MacTutor to the winter semester of 1825-26, which opened before his twenty-first birthday on 10 December 1825; the month is set to 11 to place him inside that semester. Accounts giving his age as twenty-one at these lectures are counting the academic year rather than his age at its start, and the research pool's two lenses contradicted each other on exactly this point.
stops.campa: Aged twenty, he stands up in Berlin to lecture on the theory of curves and surfaces in space. The lectures go well enough that the ministry takes notice, and what comes back is not a promotion but a direction: he will rise faster at Königsberg, four hundred miles east on the Baltic, than he will in the capital. He is advised to leave the centre in order to be advanced. Within six months he has packed. The city he leaves at twenty he will not live in again for eighteen years, and then only as an invalid.
suggested_refs: The Berlin lecture catalogues for the winter semester 1825-26
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi'

segments.name: Königsberg: the Albertina and the Elliptic Functions

stops.name: Königsberg, arrival at the Albertina as Privatdozent
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month by MacTutor, which gives May 1826; day not recorded, defaulted to 01. Coordinate inherited byte-identically from kant.journey.json for the old Albertina on the Kneiphof island beside the cathedral. The neo-Renaissance university building later associated with Königsberg was not begun until 1844, after Jacobi's years there.
stops.campa: He arrives at the Albertus University on the Kneiphof island in the Pregel, a salaried private lecturer at twenty-one, in a city whose mathematics is really Bessel's astronomy and whose winters are long. He will stay eighteen years and turn the place into the best mathematical school in Germany. The university is a set of old buildings beside the cathedral; the handsome one, the one in every later photograph, is not started until the year he leaves.
suggested_refs: The Albertina on the Kneiphof, Königsberg, as it stood before the Stueler rebuilding of 1844
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi'
kant.journey.json, Kneiphof stops, for the Albertina coordinate

stops.name: Königsberg, Bessel writes that he is here
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: Deutsche Biographie prints Bessel's letter of 12 December 1826 and Gauss's inquiry to Bessel of 20 November 1826. The German is quoted as printed and is not translated here, to avoid passing a paraphrase off as a quotation.
stops.campa: Word about the newcomer travels the German scientific network faster than the newcomer does. In November Gauss writes east asking to be told something more about this apparently very talented young man. Three weeks later Bessel, who runs the observatory here, answers that Jacobi has been in town since the beginning of the summer and draws a small salary as a private lecturer. Gauss has not met him. The answer gives the season he arrived and the size of his salary, and adds nothing else about him.
stops.quote: Jacobi ist seit Anfang des Sommers hier und bezieht, als Privatdocent, ein kleines Gehalt.
stops.quote_source: Bessel, letter of 12 December 1826, printed in Deutsche Biographie, gnd118775766
suggested_refs: Gauss's letter to Bessel of 20 November 1826 asking after Jacobi, printed in Deutsche Biographie
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi'

stops.name: Königsberg, the letter to Legendre
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: MacTutor states 'On 5 August 1827 Jacobi wrote to Legendre' and records Legendre's reply of 9 February 1828. The research pool at one point flagged this date as uncorroborated; it is not, and the flag has been dropped.
stops.campa: A twenty-two-year-old lecturer in East Prussia writes to the old man in Paris who has given forty years to elliptic integrals, to tell him what he has found. Legendre answers the following February. He is seventy-five, he has been working this same ground since before Jacobi was born, and he does not defend it: he writes that these two young men, Jacobi and the Norwegian Abel, have placed themselves among the best analysts of the era. The correspondence runs on until Legendre dies.
stops.quote: It gives me great satisfaction to see two young mathematicians such as you and [Abel] cultivate with such success a branch of analysis which for such a long time has been my favourite topic of study but which had not been received in my own country as well as it deserves. By your works you place yourselves in the ranks of the best analysts of our era.
stops.quote_source: Legendre, letter to Jacobi, 9 February 1828, translated in MacTutor History of Mathematics
suggested_refs: The Jacobi-Legendre correspondence, printed in the Gesammelte Werke
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi'

stops.name: Königsberg, extraordinary professor at twenty-three
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by MacTutor.
stops.campa: Nineteen months after arriving as a private lecturer he is made extraordinary professor, two weeks past his twenty-third birthday. The promotion is unusually fast even by the standards of a small university that can already see it will not keep him. In the same season he is writing to Gauss about cubic residues, in Latin, and to Legendre about elliptic functions, in French, from a Baltic town whose only other man of consequence in the subject runs the observatory. The date on the appointment is 28 December 1827.
suggested_refs: The Königsberg faculty records of December 1827
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi'

stops.name: Königsberg, the Fundamenta nova
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by MacTutor and English Wikipedia, for both the ordinary professorship and the book; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01. CONTRADICTION, unresolved: MacTutor alone additionally records a promotion to full professor in May 1832 after a four-hour Latin disputation, while Deutsche Biographie and both Wikipedia editions date the ordinary professorship to 1829. Both are entered in this file, at 1829 and at 1832, and neither is suppressed.
stops.campa: At twenty-four he publishes Fundamenta nova theoriae functionum ellipticarum and is made ordinary professor. The book systematizes what he and Abel have been racing each other toward: transformation theory, the modular equations, the inversion of the integrals, the theta functions. Legendre's life's treatise is superseded by two men under thirty, and Legendre, watching it happen, writes that he is glad to have lived long enough to see it. Abel dies in April of that year, at twenty-six.
stops.quote: You proceed so rapidly, gentlemen, in all these wonderful speculations that it is nearly impossible to follow you - particularly for an old man ... I congratulate myself that I have lived long enough to witness these magnanimous contests between two young equally strong athletes, who turn their efforts to the profit of the science whose limits they push back further and further.
stops.quote_source: Legendre, letter of early 1829 on the rivalry of Jacobi and Abel, translated in MacTutor History of Mathematics
suggested_refs: C. G. J. Jacobi, Fundamenta nova theoriae functionum ellipticarum (Königsberg, 1829)
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi'

stops.name: Göttingen, at the observatory with Gauss
stops.date_confidence: attested to the summer of 1829 by MacTutor and German Wikipedia; the month is set to 07 to order the journey before Paris, day defaulted to 01. Coordinate inherited byte-identically from gauss.journey.json for the Alte Sternwarte on the Geismar Landstrasse, where Gauss lived as director from 1807.
stops.campa: Travelling west for the first time in his life, he stops at Göttingen to see the man whose books he had read as a schoolboy in the Potsdam waiting room. Gauss is fifty-two, director of the observatory, hired as an astronomer and holding no chair of mathematics anywhere in Europe. The two have been writing to each other about cubic residues for two years, and this is the first time either has seen the other's face. No account records how long the visit lasted or what was said in it. Then Jacobi goes on to Paris.
suggested_refs: The Gauss-Jacobi correspondence on cubic residues, opened 1827
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi'
gauss.journey.json, observatory stop, for the coordinate

stops.name: Paris, the Institut and the men behind the books
stops.date_confidence: attested to the summer of 1829 by MacTutor and German Wikipedia; month and day are not recorded and are set to 08-01 to follow Göttingen. No source consulted names the meeting venue; the coordinate is the Institut de France pin already used in joseph_fourier.journey.json for the Academie des sciences.
stops.campa: In Paris he meets Legendre in the flesh at last, and with him Joseph Fourier and Poisson. He has come from a university where he is the entire mathematics department to the city where analysis is a public institution with a building, a salaried membership, and a printed record of its sessions. Two years of letters turn into conversation. He also collects a disagreement here that he will commit to paper within the year: Fourier holds that mathematics exists for the public utility and the explanation of nature, and Jacobi does not.
suggested_refs: The Comptes rendus and session records of the Academie des sciences for the summer of 1829
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi'

segments.name: The Honor of the Human Mind

stops.name: Königsberg, the answer to Fourier
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. Wikiquote prints the letter of 2 July 1830 to Legendre from its English translation in Science, 10 March 1911, vol. 33 no. 845, p. 359, and the text was read there directly; the archival original was not consulted for this file. Translations of the key sentence differ across sources: sole, unique, and real; mind, intellect, and spirit.
stops.campa: A year after Paris he sets it down and sends it to Legendre. Fourier thinks mathematics exists for the public utility and the explanation of natural phenomena. Jacobi answers that the unique end of science is the honor of the human mind, and that a question about number is worth exactly as much as a question about the system of the world. He is twenty-five and defending number theory against a man who has measured the heat of the earth and read the Nile. Translators since have not agreed on the words: sole, unique, or real; mind, intellect, or spirit.
stops.quote: It is true that M. Fourier had the opinion that the principal end of mathematics was the public utility and the explanation of natural phenomena; but such a philosopher as he is should have known that the unique end of science is the honor of the human mind, and that from this point of view a question of number is as important as a question of the system of the world.
stops.quote_source: Jacobi, letter to Legendre, 2 July 1830, translated in Science, 10 March 1911, vol. 33 no. 845, p. 359
suggested_refs: The shorter rendering, 'The sole end of science is the honor of the human mind,' The Mathematical Gazette, July 1905, vol. 3 no. 52, p. 200
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi'

stops.name: Königsberg, marriage to Marie Schwinck
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by MacTutor and German Wikipedia. German Wikipedia gives Marie's death as 1902 at Cannstatt; an unverified 1901 also circulates and is not followed here. The eight children are named in German Wikipedia.
stops.campa: He marries Marie Schwinck, daughter of a Königsberg merchant and commercial councillor, on the eleventh of September. There will be eight children: Leonard, George Nicolas, Jacob Adrian, August Anton Carl, Clara Margarethe, Charlotte Auguste Susanne, Marie Elisabeth Gertrud, Stephan Lejeune. The youngest carries the surname of the friend who will one day sit at his sickbed and then go and ask a king for money on his behalf. Marie outlives her husband by fifty-one years.
suggested_refs: Wikipedia (de), 'Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi', for the marriage date and the names of the eight children
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi'

stops.name: Königsberg, the four-hour disputation
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and the weakest date in this file. MacTutor alone records a promotion to full professor in May 1832 after a four-hour Latin disputation; Deutsche Biographie, German Wikipedia and English Wikipedia all date the ordinary professorship to 1829. Both cannot be a first appointment. This stop enters 1832 as a formal confirmation, which would reconcile them, but no source consulted actually says so. Day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: He argues in Latin for four hours and is confirmed in the full professorship. The record here is awkward: one biography puts the promotion at this date, three other authorities put it three years earlier, and nobody explains the gap. A confirmation after the fact would account for it. So would a plain error in one of them. The disputation itself is not in question: four hours of a dead language, defended by a man of twenty-seven. Whether the faculty listening had already given him the chair three years before, the Königsberg records would say, and nobody has read them.
suggested_refs: The Königsberg promotion records for 1829 and 1832, which would settle which reading is right
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi'

stops.name: Königsberg, the seminar with Neumann
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by MacTutor and English Wikipedia; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01. The ten hours a week of elliptic-function lectures in 1835-36 is [R], resting on the Dictionary of Scientific Biography through the research dossier and not independently refetched. Kirchhoff's attendance from 1843 to 1846 is attested by MacTutor's Kirchhoff biography.
stops.campa: With the physicist Franz Ernst Neumann he founds a mathematical-physical seminar, and it is not a lecture course. Students are handed problems nobody has solved and are expected to solve them, which is the ordinary condition of research and was then an extraordinary condition of teaching. The load Jacobi carries in these years is close to inhuman, ten hours a week on elliptic functions alone in the winter of 1835. Gustav Kirchhoff will pass through this seminar from 1843, by which time its founder is too ill to teach in it.
suggested_refs: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Gustav Robert Kirchhoff', on the Neumann-Jacobi seminar
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi'
MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Gustav Robert Kirchhoff'

segments.name: The Determinant and the Prussian Delegation

stops.name: Königsberg, Hamilton's method taken up
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from English Wikipedia, which dates Jacobi's three-body work to 1836 and the paper on first-order partial differential equations to 1837; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01. The quotation is from the Vorlesungen ueber Dynamik, lectures of 1842-43 published in 1884, and so postdates this stop by five years.
stops.campa: William Rowan Hamilton has published, in 1834 and 1835, a general method in dynamics: a whole system of moving bodies handed over to one characteristic function. Hamilton then leaves dynamics for algebra and does not come back to it. Jacobi takes the method up in Königsberg, folds the characteristic function into a broader theory of first-order partial differential equations, and finishes what the Irishman started. The equation goes under both names. They are working sequentially, not together, and have never met.
stops.quote: Any progress in the theory of partial differential equations must also bring about a progress in Mechanics.
stops.quote_source: Jacobi, Vorlesungen ueber Dynamik, lectures of 1842-43, edited by Clebsch and published Berlin 1884
suggested_refs: Hamilton's two essays on a general method in dynamics, Philosophical Transactions, 1834 and 1835

stops.name: Königsberg, the bankruptcy
stops.date_confidence: attested that Jacobi lost his money in a bankruptcy: MacTutor attributes it to a Prussia-wide and Europe-wide business depression, and Deutsche Biographie dates it to autumn 1841. Month and day defaulted to 01. The widely repeated attribution to a family bank, or to a brother Eduard's failed banking business, is NOT supported by either source and is not carried here.
stops.campa: The depression running through Prussia and Europe in the autumn takes his inherited money with it, all of it. He is thirty-six, a full professor with a wife and a growing household, and from this point he lives entirely on a salary. In November Bessel writes that they value Jacobi here doubly, not for his talent alone but for his character. Bessel writes it on the eleventh of November, within weeks of the failure, and says nothing about the money at all.
stops.quote: Wir schatzen hier J. doppelt, wegen seines Talentes nicht allein, sondern auch wegen seines Charakters.
stops.quote_source: Bessel, letter of 11 November 1841, printed in Deutsche Biographie, gnd118775766
suggested_refs: Deutsche Biographie's notice of the autumn 1841 bankruptcy, 'einen starken Bankerott'
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi'

stops.name: Königsberg, De determinantibus functionalibus
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by MacTutor for the memoir and by English Wikipedia for the notation; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: He publishes De determinantibus functionalibus, a long memoir on the determinant formed from the partial derivatives of a system of functions. It becomes the Jacobian, and it is the one object of his that reaches every later calculus course on earth. In the same period he reaches back to Legendre for the rounded d, the symbol for a partial derivative, and puts it into general use. He did not invent it. The memoir is reprinted in the Gesammelte Werke thirty years after his death.
suggested_refs: C. G. J. Jacobi, De determinantibus functionalibus (1841), reprinted in the Gesammelte Werke, ed. Borchardt, Clebsch and Weierstrass, seven volumes from 1881 with a supplement
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi'

stops.name: Manchester, the British Association
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month by MacTutor, verbatim: 'In July 1842 Jacobi and Bessel attended the meeting of the British Association for the Advancement of Science in Manchester as representatives of Prussia.' Day not recorded, defaulted to 01. Two details commonly attached to this trip are NOT supported and are excluded: that Marie Jacobi travelled with them, and that Jacobi met Hamilton there. MacTutor's Hamilton biography does not mention Jacobi at all, and English Wikipedia's Hamilton article names him only in a list of successors. Coordinate is central Manchester; no purpose-built hall existed there in 1842 and no source consulted names the venue.
stops.campa: Prussia sends two men to the British Association meeting at Manchester, and they are Bessel and Jacobi, the astronomer and the analyst, travelling together out of the same Baltic town to a mill city in the English north. It is the only time Jacobi crosses the sea. Whether he met Hamilton there, whose dynamics he had completed five years earlier, is exactly the sort of thing every retelling asserts and no source consulted supports. He is thirty-seven, at the height of his powers, with less than a year of health left.
suggested_refs: The Report of the Twelfth Meeting of the British Association for the Advancement of Science, Manchester, June 1842
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi'

stops.name: Paris, lecturing on the way home
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and thin. Lectures at Paris on the return journey appear in the research dossier's own itinerary table and were corroborated by no source independently fetched for this file. Month and day are set only to follow the attested Manchester stop.
stops.campa: On the way back from England he stops in Paris and lectures. It is thirteen years since he first came here as a provincial with one book to his name; he is now the most famous working mathematician in Germany, and the city that taught him analysis in print sits and listens. If it happened, it is the last thing he does outside Germany. The stop rests on one uncorroborated line in an itinerary table, and no Paris session record naming him in August 1842 has been found.
suggested_refs: Any Paris session record of August 1842 naming Jacobi, which would confirm or kill this stop
sources: joseph_fourier.journey.json, Academie des sciences stops, for the Paris coordinate

stops.name: Königsberg, the collapse
stops.date_confidence: attested: MacTutor and German Wikipedia both record the 1843 diabetes diagnosis, and German Wikipedia has him giving up his Königsberg lectures for reasons of health before the Italian journey, which places the onset here and not in Berlin as the research pool first had it. Month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01. English Wikipedia's summary instead describes a mental breakdown from overwork; no source consulted reconciles the two descriptions. There is no conflict with the 1851 smallpox death: MacTutor carries both, eight years apart.
stops.campa: The load he has been carrying since the seminar began, ten years of it, comes due. He falls seriously ill and the diagnosis is diabetes; another account calls it a collapse from overwork, and nobody reconciles the two. He is thirty-eight. He gives up his lectures for reasons of health. Kirchhoff arrives in the seminar that same year and is trained by Neumann, because the other founder is in bed. He has been at Königsberg eighteen years. He does not lecture there again.
suggested_refs: Leo Koenigsberger, Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi (Leipzig, 1904), the centenary biography, not consulted directly for this file
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi'

stops.name: Königsberg, Dirichlet at the bedside and the king's money
stops.date_confidence: the Dirichlet visit and the appeal through Alexander von Humboldt to King Friedrich Wilhelm IV are attested by MacTutor. The month of April and the 'roughly two weeks' duration come from the research dossier via Koenigsberger's 1904 biography and are NOT independently confirmed; day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet comes east and sits with him. Then he goes to Alexander von Humboldt, who has been Prussian science's broker at court since his return to Berlin in 1827, and Humboldt goes to Friedrich Wilhelm IV, and the king pays for a winter in Italy. Jacobi cannot pay for it himself; the bankruptcy of 1841 took everything he had. The convalescence that saves his life is a favour arranged by two friends and granted by a monarch he will publicly embarrass five years later.
suggested_refs: The Prussian cabinet order granting Jacobi the Italian travel funds, 1843
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi'

stops.name: Lucca, the congress and the unread papers
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by MacTutor for the Lucca meeting; no month is given, and 10 is set only to order this stop before the attested arrival at Rome on 16 November 1843. That few Italian mathematicians had seriously read his papers is a secondary-source observation carried from the research dossier and not independently verified.
stops.campa: He travels south with Dirichlet, with Dirichlet's wife, and with Carl Wilhelm Borchardt, and stops at a scientific congress in Lucca. The report that comes back is that he found few Italian mathematicians who had seriously read him. He is thirty-eight and the author of the Fundamenta nova, and in Tuscany he is a name on a list. The party does not stay. It goes on south toward Rome, four Germans travelling on a doctor's orders at the pace of an invalid.
suggested_refs: The proceedings of the Italian scientific congress at Lucca, 1843
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi'

stops.name: Rome, the arrival and the circle
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by MacTutor, which also names Steiner and Schlaefli as joining the party in Rome.
stops.campa: They reach Rome on the sixteenth of November. Jakob Steiner joins the party there, and Ludwig Schlaefli, whose command of languages makes him the group's interpreter. For most of a year a good part of the German mathematical elite is quartered in a papal city, taking the winter air on a Prussian king's grant, with the sickest of them slowly improving. Dirichlet is here, and Borchardt, who will one day edit the collected works. Nobody in Rome is asking any of them to teach anything. They stay until the following summer.
suggested_refs: Schlaefli's later account of the Roman winter of 1843-44
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi'

stops.name: Rome, the Vatican Library and Diophantus
stops.date_confidence: attested by German Wikipedia that Jacobi collated manuscripts of Diophantus in the Vatican Library during the Italian stay; no date within 1843-1844 is given, and 1844-01-01 is set to order the stop after the attested Rome arrival.
stops.campa: In the Vatican Library he works on the manuscripts of Diophantus's Arithmetica, comparing readings. The Greek is not an ornament: he was certified to teach it at nineteen and has never stopped reading it. A man sent abroad specifically to stop working spends his mornings collating a third-century text on indeterminate equations, which is number theory, the subject he had told Legendre was worth as much as the system of the world. No source dates the work within the Roman stay.
suggested_refs: The Vatican Library's Greek manuscripts of Diophantus, Arithmetica

stops.name: Berlin, the return as a state pensioner
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month by MacTutor and English Wikipedia, which have him back in Berlin by the end of June 1844; day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: He comes back to Berlin by the end of June, improved, and does not go back to Königsberg. The physicians hold the Baltic climate dangerous for him and the crown permits a permanent transfer: he becomes a royal pensioner in the capital, with a supplement for the higher cost of living and for his medicines. It is the arrangement of a man who has been bought out of one life and set down in another. He is thirty-nine and holds no chair anywhere, in Prussia or outside it.
suggested_refs: The royal permission of 1844 transferring Jacobi from Königsberg to Berlin as a pensioner
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi'

stops.campa: Volume one of the Opuscula mathematica goes out with a dedication to Friedrich Wilhelm IV, in the register of loyalty and gratitude that a pensioner owes the man paying the pension. It is also simply true, on the record, that the king had paid for the winter in Rome that kept him alive. Two years later Jacobi will stand up in a liberal club in this same city and say things that cost him the money. The dedication is not withdrawn, and volume one keeps it.

stops.name: Berlin, the lectures on analytical mechanics
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; MacTutor places lectures on analytical mechanics at Berlin in 1847-48. The course survives only through Wilhelm Scheibner's student notes and was not published until 1996, so the quotation is his lecture-room wording as reconstructed from a hearer, not from an autograph. Month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: He lectures in Berlin on analytical mechanics and a student named Scheibner writes it down. The notebook is printed a hundred and forty-nine years later. In it he warns the room that wherever mathematics gets mixed up with something outside its own field, somebody will try to demonstrate a merely conventional proposition a priori, and it will be their job to find the false step. He is teaching suspicion of his own instrument to men who came to learn how to use it. What survives of the course is Scheibner's hand. Of Jacobi's own there is nothing.
stops.quote: Wherever Mathematics is mixed up with anything, which is outside its field, you will find attempts to demonstrate these merely conventional propositions a priori, and it will be your task to find out the false deduction in each case.
stops.quote_source: Jacobi, Vorlesungen ueber analytische Mechanik: Berlin 1847/48, edited from Wilhelm Scheibner's notes and published 1996
suggested_refs: Vorlesungen ueber analytische Mechanik: Berlin 1847/48, ed. from Scheibner's notes (1996)
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi'

stops.name: Berlin, the Constitutional Club
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by MacTutor for the club and the speech, and by English Wikipedia for an unsuccessful Liberal parliamentary candidacy in 1848. A February date circulates and is NOT followed here: MacTutor gives no month, and the Berlin rising did not begin until March. Month and day defaulted to 01. The refusal of his request to join the Berlin university staff is dated by MacTutor only as following the political activity.
stops.campa: The revolution reaches Berlin in March, and Jacobi joins the liberal Constitutional Club and makes an impromptu speech. It offends everyone: too liberal for the conservative authorities, not radical enough for the left. No source preserves a word of what he actually said; the state records only the effect. Some time afterward his request to join the staff of the University of Berlin is refused. He stands as a Liberal candidate that same year and loses.
suggested_refs: Records of the Berlin Konstitutioneller Klub, 1848
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi'

stops.name: Berlin, the supplement withdrawn
stops.date_confidence: attested by MacTutor that the salary supplement was withdrawn and the family moved to Gotha 'by the summer of 1849'; no month is given and 06 is set to place the stop in that summer. Three details often attached here are NOT in MacTutor or Deutsche Biographie and are excluded: that he gave up his house, that he lodged in an inn, and that the ruin was a brother Eduard's failed bank. The eight children are attested by German Wikipedia.
stops.campa: The revolution is beaten and the accounting starts. The government withdraws the supplement to his pension. With no inherited money since 1841 and a household of ten, he cannot keep them in the capital: Marie and the eight children go to Gotha, where living is cheap, and he stays in Berlin. He is forty-four, the most internationally famous mathematician Prussia has, and he has now been made poor twice by things that had nothing to do with mathematics.
suggested_refs: The Prussian ministerial file on Jacobi's pension supplement, 1844 to 1849
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi'

stops.name: Berlin, the Vienna chair
stops.date_confidence: the offer and its withdrawal are attested by MacTutor; the date is not. MacTutor gives only 'a few months later' after the summer of 1849, and German Wikipedia dates the Vienna professorship offer to 1850. The range is late 1849 to 1850 and is deliberately not narrowed. Month and day defaulted to 01. The stop sits at Berlin because that is where Jacobi was; he never took up the Vienna chair.
stops.campa: Vienna offers him a chair and he provisionally accepts it. The offer falls somewhere between late 1849 and 1850, and the sources do not narrow it. The prospect of Prussia losing its most famous living mathematician to Austria does what his poverty could not: the government produces concessions, and his position in Berlin improves at once. He withdraws the acceptance and stays, preferring, he says, his own country. Was the offer ever anything more than the lever he needed? The record does not answer, and he never sees Vienna.
suggested_refs: The Vienna appointment correspondence of 1849-1850
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi'

stops.name: Berlin, the summer semester on number theory
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from MacTutor, which records lectures on number theory in the summer semester of 1850; the month is set to 04 to place the stop at the opening of that semester, day defaulted to 01. The quotation is [R]: it is later testimony reported by Schubring, not a Jacobi autograph, and the wording here follows MacTutor's printing exactly, including its trailing ellipsis. Three common misquotations of it are avoided.
stops.campa: His position restored, he lectures at Berlin in the summer semester on the theory of numbers, the subject he had defended to Legendre twenty years earlier as worth as much as the system of the world. He is forty-five. By the report of his students he is also saying in these Berlin years that neither he nor Cauchy nor Gauss knows what a completely rigorous proof is, and that only Dirichlet does. The remark reaches us secondhand, through a hearer, and no autograph of it exists.
stops.quote: Dirichlet alone, not I, nor Cauchy, nor Gauss knows what a completely rigorous mathematical proof is. Rather we learn it first from him. When Gauss says that he has proved something, it is very clear; when Cauchy says it, one can wager as much pro as con; when Dirichlet says it, it is certain ...
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Jacobi in G. Schubring, Zur Modernisierung des Studiums der Mathematik in Berlin, as printed on MacTutor's Jacobi quotations page; later testimony, not an autograph

stops.name: Gotha, the summer with the family
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; MacTutor records that he spent the summer vacation of 1850 with his family, who were still living at Gotha. The month is set to 07 for a summer vacation, day defaulted to 01. The detail that the family stayed on until the eldest son finished his Gymnasium comes from the research dossier and was not independently refetched.
stops.campa: He goes to Gotha for the vacation, to the small Thuringian town where Marie and the eight children have been living for a year because the capital costs too much. The plan is that they stay until the eldest boy finishes his Gymnasium, and everyone involved treats the arrangement as temporary. He has been separated from his household by a political speech. He goes back to Berlin alone in the autumn. The family is still at Gotha the following February.
suggested_refs: The Gotha residence of the Jacobi family, 1849 to 1851
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi'

stops.name: Berlin, influenza and then smallpox
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month by MacTutor: influenza in January 1851, then smallpox before he had regained his strength. Day not recorded, defaulted to 01. A claim that the influenza was caught while visiting the family at Gotha is NOT supported by any source consulted and is excluded.
stops.campa: In January he catches influenza. A claim that he caught it visiting the family at Gotha runs through later retellings and appears in no source consulted. He is still weak from it, not yet back on his feet, when he contracts smallpox. He is forty-six, and this is his second grave illness in eight years. Eight years earlier a king's money had bought him a winter in Rome and with it his life; this time nothing is arranged, and nothing can be. No source names who was in the room with him.
suggested_refs: Berlin municipal smallpox records for the winter of 1850-51
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi'

stops.name: Berlin, death
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by MacTutor and both Wikipedia editions; English Wikipedia specifies smallpox as the cause. Dirichlet's Gedaechtnissrede is attested by Deutsche Biographie only as published in the Berlin Academy's Abhandlungen for 1852; a delivery date of 1 July 1852, and the wording 'the greatest mathematician since Lagrange', appear in no source consulted and are excluded.
stops.campa: He dies on the eighteenth of February, a few days after the pox takes hold, at forty-six. Dirichlet, who had sat at his bedside in Königsberg eight years before and then gone to a king on his behalf, writes the Academy's memorial address; it appears in the Abhandlungen for 1852. His collected works will take the Berlin Academy seven volumes and a supplementary volume, and the printing begins in 1881. His wife and his eight children are at Gotha, where they have lived since 1849.

stops.name: Berlin-Kreuzberg, the iron cross at Baruther Strasse
stops.date_confidence: the burial place is attested by both Wikipedia editions: Friedhof I der Dreifaltigkeits-Kirchengemeinde, Baruther Strasse 61 in Kreuzberg, grave DV2-SA-1T, marked by a pedestalled iron cross, made an Ehrengrab of the State of Berlin in 1980 and renewed in 2001 for twenty years. The exact burial date is NOT recorded; 20 February is set only to follow the attested death. The coordinate is disputed in the research pool, which supplied 52.4879/13.3897 from one lens and 52.4903/13.3862 from another for the same grave. Both were rejected and the figure here is re-derived from the Baruther Strasse 61 address; no source consulted publishes the cemetery's own coordinate.
stops.campa: They bury him in the Trinity parish's first cemetery, off the Baruther Strasse south of the old Hallesches Tor, under a plain iron cross on a pedestal. In the neighbouring ground, the second cemetery of the Jerusalem and New Church parishes, lies Encke of the Berlin observatory. In 1904 the mathematician H. A. Schwarz has to publish an article establishing where the grave actually is, in the same year as Koenigsberger's centenary biography. Berlin makes it a protected honorary grave in 1980.
suggested_refs: H. A. Schwarz, 'Die Grabstaette J.'s', Jahresbericht der Deutschen Mathematiker-Vereinigung (1904)
